memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Build there an altar to the Lord your God, an altar of stones. Do not use any iron tool on them. Build the altar of the Lord your God with fieldstones and offer burnt offerings on it to the Lord your God." — Deut 27:5-6 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
When Israel built an altar to worship God, they were to use natural, uncut fieldstones — no iron tool touched them. Why such a specific command? Because the altar was about God's provision, not human craftsmanship. The moment a person began chiselling and shaping, they might start admiring their own work rather than worshipping God. The rough, plain stones kept the focus where it belonged.

There is a lesson here about how we come to God. We are tempted to think we must polish ourselves up, add our own improvements, contribute something impressive before God will accept us. But the altar of plain stones says otherwise. We come to God on His terms, bringing nothing of our own cleverness to boast in.

This points beautifully to the gospel. Salvation is not something we build or improve with our own "tools." It is God's provision from start to finish, so that no one can boast (Eph 2:8-9). The cross of Christ is the true altar, and there we bring no contribution of our own — only empty hands of faith.

So come to God as you are. Stop chiselling, stop trying to make yourself acceptable by your own effort. Worship rests on what God has provided, not on what you can craft.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Am I trying to "improve myself" to earn God's acceptance?
2. Where might I be tempted to boast in my own spiritual efforts?
3. How does the cross free me from having to impress God?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, I come to You with empty hands, not trusting my own efforts but Your provision alone. Thank You that salvation is Your gift, not my achievement. Amen.
